paper_title: Dynamic Important Example Mining for Reinforcement Finetuning

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) is increasingly used to strengthen the reasoning abilities of large models, yet its effectiveness is bound by how training data are selected and used. Most data-centric RFT methods rely on static or heuristic sample selection, implicitly assuming a sample's value is fixed over training. This overlooks the non-stationary dynamics of policy learning and can lead to suboptimal updates. We propose Dynamic Important Example Mining (DIEM), a principled and fully automated framework that makes data utilization adaptive throughout RFT. DIEM integrates two components into each optimization step: (i) a gradient-alignment importance estimator that efficiently approximates each sample's marginal contribution to policy improvement; and (ii) a constrained batch reweighting scheme that maximizes aggregate utility while preserving the update's gradient magnitude to stabilize optimization. Across several reasoning benchmarks, DIEM consistently outperforms strong static and dynamic baselines. The code will be released via https://github.com/hrtan/DIEM.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Reinforcement Fine-Tuning (RFT) has recently emerged as key paradigm for enhancing the reasoning and alignment capabilities of large-scale visionlanguage models (Tong et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024b; Bai et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2024b; Zhu et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025a; Li et al., 2024) and language models (Guo et al., 2025; OpenAI, 2024; Team et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2025). By integrating reinforcement learning into the post-training stage, RFT allows models to learn directly from reward signals, refining their decision-making beyond supervised imitation (Chu et al., 2025a). However, the effectiveness of RFT critically depends on how data is utilized during policy optimization (Guo et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2025). The selection, ordering, and weighting of training samples fundamentally determine both the stability of optimization and the generalization of reasoning abilities. Despite RFTs inherently dynamic, non-stationary nature, most existing data-centric approaches overlook this dynamism, treating data importance as fixed throughout training. These methods typically pre-select samples using heuristic indicators such as reward variance (Wang et al., 2025b) or difficulty (Li et al., 2025). While such strategies can improve data efficiency, they suffer from critical limitation: the assumption that samples contribution remains constant across the entire learning trajectory. Recent advances in reinforcement learning (Gao et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025b; Yu et al., 2025) have begun to explore dynamic sample weighting and curriculum scheduling within the RFT framework. For example, Prompt Curriculum Learning (PCL) (Gao et al., 2025) introduces an auxiliary value model to estimate sample difficulty, while SPEED-RL (Zhang et al., 2025b) prioritizes data with intermediate pass rates to maintain balanced learning progression. However, such heuristic metrics Personal Email: hrtan@eee.hku.hk : Corresponding author: Sitong Wu and Xiaojuan Qi. 1 Figure 1: The pipeline of our proposed dynamic important example mining (DIEM). Compared with the vanilla RFT pipeline, our DIEM introduces only two lightweight steps: (1) Dynamic Data Importance Measuring, which evaluates the importance of each sample within the current batch using our proposed influence estimator in Eq.4; and (2) Dynamic Data Reweighting, which reallocates sample weights based on their importance. The reweighting step is formulated as constrained optimization problem that preserves the overall gradient magnitude while emphasizing the most important samples (defined in Eq.6, and we further provide an efficient closed-form solution in Eq.7). Overall, DIEM is highly efficient, intuitive, and broadly compatible with existing RFT algorithms (Shao et al., 2024; Hu, 2025; Schulman et al., 2017; 2015). (e.g., difficulty score) fail to capture two essential aspects. First, they do not accurately reflect the policys intrinsic preference or fitness for given sample, since the judgment is made externally, detached from the policy itself. Second, they cannot quantify samples true marginal impact on policy updates, which is crucial for understanding and optimizing the contribution of each example to reasoning improvement. To address these limitations, we propose Dynamic Important Example Mining (DIEM), principled and fully automated framework that explicitly models the dynamic contribution of each training sample during the RFT process. Unlike previous heuristic-based methods, DIEM integrates data importance estimation directly into the policy optimization loop, making data utilization an adaptive component of learning rather than fixed pretraining stage. At every optimization step, DIEM quantifies how much each sample contributes to the current policy improvement and dynamically reweights its influence in subsequent updates. This continuous adjustment transforms data selection from one-time preprocessing step into self-organizing, curriculum-like mechanism driven entirely by model dynamics. Specifically, DIEM consists of two key components executed at every RFT iteration: (1) Dynamic Data Importance Measuring and (2) Dynamic Data Reweighting. For importance measuring, our approach departs from heuristic criteria such as difficulty or entropy (Toneva et al., 2018; Cody Coleman et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2025b; Gao et al., 2025) and instead introduces theoretically grounded, gradient-based estimator that directly evaluates each samples marginal contribution to policy improvement. The estimator computes the alignment between the samples gradient and the aggregated batch gradient, providing an efficient and mathematically guaranteed proxy for true importance. For data reweighting, we formulate constrained optimization problem that maximizes the batchs aggregate contribution while maintaining consistent gradient magnitude, thereby stabilizing the optimization trajectory and avoiding large step-size fluctuations. This joint mechanism converts data selection into an intrinsic part of RFT, enabling adaptive curriculum formation and stable credit assignment throughout training. We extensively evaluate DIEM on large-scale multimodal reasoning benchmarks. Across all benchmarks, DIEM consistently outperforms strong static and dynamic baselines, providing significant performance uplift to the base RFT algorithm of approximately 1%6%, while introducing only minimal additional 1.2% training overhead. Moreover, DIEM demonstrates broad compatibility with diverse RFT algorithms (Shao et al., 2024; Schulman et al., 2015; 2017; Hu, 2025), confirming its general applicability. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this dynamic reweighting intrinsically induces powerful, self-organizing curriculum learning paradigm (Sec. 5.5). 2 We summarize our primary contributions as follows: 1. We introduce novel, theoretically-grounded, fully automated, and highly efficient dynamic data selection framework that significantly boosts the performance of RFT with negligible computational overhead. 2. We develop dynamic importance indicator based on gradient-based alignment to precisely quantify the marginal contribution of individual samples, moving decisively beyond static or heuristic scoring methods. 3. DIEM consistently achieves the best performance with minimal additional 1.2% training overhead. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this dynamic reweighting intrinsically induces powerful, self-organizing curriculum learning paradigm (Sec. 5.5).

sections.title: 2 Related Works
sections.content: Reinforcement Fine-Tuning. The rapid surge in the performance of Large Models (OpenAI, 2024; Guo et al., 2025; Team et al., 2025) is largely attributable to Reinforcement Fine-Tuning (RFT). This optimization paradigm refines model behavior through reinforcement learning, leveraging reward signals to steer the model towards desired outputs. The canonical RFT pipeline, particularly for aligning LLMs with human values, is Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) (Christiano et al., 2023; Ouyang et al., 2022). Recent advancements have diversified RFT away from the conventional RLHF with external RMs. For instance, in tasks such as complex reasoning and code generation, RFT can use verifiable rewards, where the reward is direct, objective signal of correctness, such as pass/fail from unit test or mathematical proof check (Shao et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2025). DeepSeek-R1 (Guo et al., 2025) is prominent example, employing Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) (Shao et al., 2024) with binary rewards to achieve state-of-the-art results. Much of the contemporary RFT research focuses on algorithmic refinements to the standard PPO/RLHF process. For example, DAPO and GPG (Yu et al., 2025; Chu et al., 2025b) have sought to simplify GRPO for more robust empirical performance in certain settings. Numerous studies are also applying Reinforcement Fine-Tuning (RFT) to multimodal reasoning (Huang et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025a; Meng et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025a; Peng et al., 2025; Zhan et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025d). Examples of these contributions include the proposal of high-quality and diverse RFT datasets (Meng et al., 2025), the design of step-wise supervision signals like R1-VL (Zhang et al., 2025a), and the development of cost-efficient training pipelines (Chen et al., 2025b). Data Selection in RFT. Most contemporary data-centric strategies for RFT aim to identify high-value samples and are broadly divided into two categories: 1. Static Selection: These methods (Li et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025b) curate the training subset before RFT begins, relying on one-time analysis of reward trends or variability. For instance, LIMR (Li et al., 2025) selects samples by analyzing changes in reward trends, indicating significant opportunities for policy improvement. Historical Variance Score HVS (Wang et al., 2025b) prioritizes data exhibiting high reward variability, based on the intuition that instability signals high optimization impact. Their critical flaw is the underlying assumption that samples importance remains constant throughout the entire non-stationary training process. 2. Dynamic Selection: Inspired by curriculum learning, these methods (Zeng et al., 2025; Ji et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2025) dynamically reorder samples, often prioritizing examples of intermediate difficulty. PCL (Gao et al., 2025) trains an auxiliary value model to serve as an external difficulty evaluator. SPEED-RL (Zhang et al., 2025b) uses the pass rate of samples as an importance indicator, often prioritizing medium-difficulty examples. However, because they rely on heuristic metrics external to the core policy optimization, they fail to accurately reflect the policys true internal preference or the samples genuine marginal contribution to the final policy update.

sections.title: 3 Preliminaries
sections.content: We now formalize the application of Reinforcement Learning (RL) to the finetuning of Large Models (Llama Team, 2024; Team, 2024), process commonly referred to as Reinforcement Fine-Tuning (RFT) (OpenAI, 2024; Guo et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2025; Shao et al., 2024; Yuan et al., 2025; Team et al., 2025). The training corpus is denoted as tzi : psi, yiquN i1, consisting of input-output pairs, where si represents prompt or query and yi is its solution. In domains such as mathematical reasoning, yi typically corresponds to deterministic ground-truth answer. The LLM acts as stochastic policy πθ, parameterized by θ. Within this framework, the input query serves as the observation (state), and the generated text corresponds to the chosen action. The quality of is evaluated via scalar feedback signal the reward r. The objective of RFT is to iteratively optimize πθ such that it generates high-fidelity, desirable responses (Schulman et al., 2017; Shao et al., 2024). This is typically instantiated by assigning 1 for exact matches with the target yi and 1 for incorrect or suboptimal generations. Vanilla Policy Optimization. The fundamental goal of RFT is realized by maximizing the expected empirical advantage over sampled state-action pairs ps, aq. This constitutes the simplest Policy Gradient optimization criterion and the corresponding policy gradient: pθq ps,aq ı , Aps, aq θJ pθq ps,aq Aps, aq θ log πθpasq ı , (1) where the advantage function is defined as Aps, aq rps, aq v. This term quantifies the relative merit of executing action in state compared to learned or predefined baseline value v. Optimization proceeds via iterative stochastic gradient ascent: θt`1 θt ` ηtθ Jpθtq, where the step size is governed by the learning rate ηt. Beyond the Vanilla Policy Gradient. To circumvent the inherent instability associated with simple gradient ascent, contemporary RFT architectures commonly integrate refined optimization schemes, like Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) (Schulman et al., 2017), Quantile-Based Policy Optimization (QPO) (Jiang et al., 2022), Group Policy Gradient (GPG) (Chu et al., 2025b), Dynamic Sampling Policy Optimization (Yu et al., 2025). Among them, Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) (Shao et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2025) has emerged as one of the most influential techniques and now serves as the foundation for many RFT pipelines (Yu et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025; Yuan et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025c). GRPO extends PPO by computing the advantage through intra-group comparisons of outputs generated for single prompt s. Rather than training separate value model to estimate the baseline v, GRPO samples small set of responses ta1, . . . , aGu from the old policy πθold . The GRPO objective retains the PPO-style clipping mechanism and is formulated as: GRPOpθq ps,aiq clip πθpaisq πθold paisq 1 Gÿ min i1 πθpaisq πθold paisq Aps, aiq, , 1 ϵ, 1 ` ϵ Aps, aiq βKL pπθ}πrefq ı , (2) where, the advantage term Aps, aiq is calculated based on the standardized reward within the collected group, defined as Aps, aiq rimeanpr1,...,rGq , where ri is the reward for output ai. The clipping operator truncates excessively large or small relative advantage values, thereby ensuring smoother and more stable optimization process. This standardization fundamentally bypasses the need for separate value function, simplifying the training process. sections.title: 4 Dynamic Important Example Mining
sections.content: The core idea of our Dynamic Important Example Mining (DIEM) is to assess the importance of the current batch of data at each step of the RFT process and adjust the weight of each sample accordingly. Section 4.1 will present our theoretically grounded strategy for measuring sample importance. Section 4.2 will describe the sample re-weighting strategy, and finally, Section 4.3 will give an overview of the entire algorithm. 4.1 Dynamic Data Importance Measuring We begin by introducing principled formulation for quantifying the contribution of each training sample to the models learning dynamics. Unlike heuristic methods that rely on ad hoc proxies such as reward variance or difficulty, our approach provides formal and theoretically justified estimate of each samples true influence on policy improvement. Problem Definition. Let Bt denote the training minibatch sampled at RFT step t, and let Bt be an individual sample. We use Btztzu to denote the batch with sample removed. Let θt be the policy parameters before the update at step t. The performance metric we consider is the Total Batch Reward achieved by the policy after one gradient update. We define the importance score Itpzq of sample at step as the change in the total batch reward, evaluated on the original batch Bt, that results from removing from the update calculation (Koh & Liang, 2017; Hara et al., 2019; Pruthi et al., 2020; Tan et al., 2025b;a): Itpzq θupdate Bt , Bt θupdate Btztzu , Bt , (3) where θupdate is the policy πθt after single gradient step calculated on batch B. This metric offers precise, non-heuristic measure of utility. positive Itpzq indicates that including sample in the update led to better performing policy on the current batchs reward, suggesting is beneficial for that specific step. Conversely, negative Itpzq implies zs inclusion caused detrimental policy shift relative to the batchs total reward, suggesting it is harmful at this moment. Scores near zero denote negligible marginal influence. This directional score thus serves as an interpretable indicator for dynamic sample reweighting. 4.1.1 Efficient Estimation The direct computation of Itpzq as defined in Eq. (3) is intractable. Calculating Itpzq for batch of size Bt necessitates at least Bt times of full gradient updates and evaluation, cost that renders the method unusable in high-throughput training environments. To address this severe computational bottleneck, we introduce an Efficient First-order Gradient Alignment Estimator that serves as highly effective, low-cost proxy for Itpzq. This estimator determines samples instantaneous value by quantifying the degree to which its policy gradient contributes to the collective batch update direction. Proposition 1. (Gradient Alignment Estimator) We define the estimated importance score ˆItpzq for sample Bt at step using the inner product between its individual policy gradient and the total aggregate policy gradient of the batch: ˆItpzq ηt where the inner product x, measures vector alignment. Unlike static data selection pipelines that require pre-training and subset formation, our method continuously modulates sample contributions throughout the entire training process, as detailed in Algorithm 1. sections.title: 5 Experiments
sections.content: In Sec. 5.1 and Sec. 5.2, we report the main results across visual and mathematical reasoning benchmarks. Finally, we provide two dedicated analyses: an ablation study in Sec. 5.3 and visualization in Sec. 5.5. 5.1 LLM Results All algorithms are implemented via the veRL framework using open-source Qwen series models, and trained on cluster of 16 NVIDIA H200 GPUs. We compare our approach against GRPO (Shao et al., 2024), LIMR (Li et al., 2025), and HVS (Wang et al., 2025b) baselines. For the GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) baseline, we disable the KL penalty and entropy bonus, utilizing clipping ratio of 0.2. The training configurations include prompt batch size of 64, 8 rollouts per prompt, mini-batch size of 32, and micro-batch size of 8 (reduced to 4 for 7B/8B models). The maximum prompt and response lengths are set to 1,024 and 2,048 tokens, respectively. We optimize the models with constant learning rate of 1e-6 and no warmup. The one exception is AMC-23 on Qwen3-4B, where DIEM scores 55.0 compared to GRPOs 58.5; this appears to be an outlier specific to this modelbenchmark pair, as DIEM improves AMC-23 on all other models. For training data, we randomly sampled 52K multimodal entries from the MM-Eureka corpus (Meng et al., 2025). The 7B model was trained on 16 NVIDIA A100 GPUs, and the 32B model on 32 GPUs. The reinforcement learning phase utilized global batch size of 128 and learning rate of 1 ˆ 106. We evaluate the performance of our models across comprehensive suite of challenging multimodal benchmarks, covering both general reasoning and specialized mathematical problem-solving. Our evaluation set includes MathVista (Lu et al., 2023), MathVerse (Zhang et al., 2024a), MathVision (Wang et al., 2024b), MMStar (Chen et al., 2024a), MMMU (Yue et al., 2024), AI2D (Kembhavi et al., 2016). We choose several baselines as competitors to our approach, including static selection methods, including HVS (Wang et al., 2025b) and LIMR (Li et al., 2025), and dynamic methods, including PCL (Gao et al., 2025) and SPEED-RL (Zhang et al., 2025b). In addition, we also chose random selection as the most classic baseline. The main experimental results, comparing our proposed DIEM algorithm against various state-of-the-art data selection methods and strong commercial models, are summarized in Table 2. Across the 7B model family, our proposed DIEM algorithm achieves superior average performance of 61.8% across all six evaluated benchmarks, demonstrating its effectiveness in dynamic sample selection during RFT. This result represents significant gain of 3.6 percentage points over the Vanilla RFT baseline (59.1%) and 1.8 percentage points over the best-performing existing data selection Figure 2: The speed test of various data selection methods when combined with Vanilla RFT (GRPO) (Shao et al., 2024). method, SPEED-RL (60.0%) (Zhang et al., 2025b). Specifically, DIEM secures the highest scores in five out of six benchmarks, including MathVista (76.9%), MathVerse (53.0%), MathVision (28.7%), MMStar (67.9%), and AI2D (85.0%). Notably, DIEMs performance on the average benchmark score (61.8%) also surpasses the average score of the powerful commercial model GPT-4o (60.9%), highlighting the efficiency and power of our data reweighting mechanism even on much smaller base model. The performance advantage of DIEM is consistently maintained and further amplified when applied to the larger Qwen2.5-VL-32B base model. DIEM achieves leading average score of 67.3%, which is an improvement of 2.4 percentage points over the Vanilla RFT baseline (64.9%) and gain of 1.7 percentage points over the previous best dynamic baseline, SPEED-RL (65.6%). For the 32B model, DIEM demonstrates dominance across all six individual benchmarks, achieving the highest score in every category. This comprehensive superiority underscores the ability of DIEM to consistently identify and prioritize high-value training samples, leading to more robust and effective policy optimization across diverse multimodal reasoning tasks, especially within higher-capacity models. 5.3 Ablation Study Table 3 presents an ablation study validating the contribution of DIEMs two core components against the full models 58.0 performance. The first group of studies indicates that substituting our dynamic influence score with alternative metrics resulted in significant performance drops. Random value replacement or using the raw Pass@k score (Zhang et al., 2025b) caused deficits of 5.0 (to 53.0) and 4.8 points (to 53.2), respectively. The largest drop was 5.9 points (to 52.1) when using the raw PCL Difficulty score (Gao et al., 2025). While translating these alternative scores to the distance to the median offered some improvement (e.g., Pass@k distance gained 1.7 points, reaching 54.9), none approached our method, confirming the superiority of our dynamic scoring approach. The second group of studies indicates that our reweighting function is essential. Removing this step entirely (NULL-operation) dropped performance by 2.6 points (to 55.4). Replacing it with standard Softmax normalization resulted in 1.6 point deficit (to 56.4). This confirms that our specialized reweighting function is critical for maximizing benefit from the influence scores. In summary, both the dynamic data influence score and the custom data reweighting step are indispensable components, jointly contributing to the superior 58.0 performance. 5.4 Speed Test DIEM offers significant speed advantage, see Fig. 2. Unlike traditional, static data selection models that demand time-consuming, resource-intensive training of separate surrogate model on all data, our dynamic DIEM method eliminates this requirement. The speed test results confirm this efficiency: integrating DIEM with the baseline Vanilla RFT (GRPO) framework introduces only minimal overhead. The baseline takes 70.3 hours, while the combined DIEM system requires just 10 Table 3: Ablation study on MathVerse (Zhang et al., 2024a) with Qwen-2.5-VL-32B (Bai et al., 2025) as the base model. Results on more benchmarks could be seen in the supplementary materials. Replace the data reweighting step with: Performance No Replacement (Ours) NULL-operation Softmax normalization 58.0 55.4 56.4 71.2 hours, an increase of only 0.9 hours (about 1.28%). This marginal increase is significantly lower than all other state-of-the-art methods tested, such as PCL (79.1 hours), SPEED-RL (94.6 hours), and especially LIMR and HVS (both 122.0 hours). This superior efficiency stems from DIEMs design: it avoids separate inference or dedicated training steps for surrogate model or data selector. Instead, DIEM operates solely by leveraging and reusing the gradient information already computed during the original RFT algorithms standard update cycle. 5.5 Training Process Visualization To quantify this evolution, we use Pass@k as proxy for sample difficulty and group examples into Hard, Medium, and Easy categories (lower Pass@k implies higher difficulty). We then track the DIEM-assigned relative weights of these groups over training, as shown in Fig. 3. The results reveal that DIEM naturally introduces smooth curriculum learning trend. During the initial training stages, both the Easy and Medium difficulty groups are assigned relatively high importance weights. However, as training progresses, the weight assigned to the Easy samples rapidly declines, indicating that the model has saturated its learning potential from these examples. Simultaneously, the weight trajectory of the Hard group shows sustained increase, though accompanied by oscillations, as the model shifts its focus to more challenging samples. This easy-to-hard progression emerges organically, in sharp contrast to prior methods (Gao et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025b) that rely on rigid, hand-designed heuristics to adjust sample priority. Such heuristic approaches are often brittle and fail to reflect the models evolving state, leading to less efficient learning. Figure 3: Normalized weight trajectories of different difficulty samples (groups) during DIEM Training.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: We introduced the Dynamic Important Example Mining (DIEM) framework for enhancing Reinforcement Fine-Tuning (RFT) of large models. DIEM moves beyond fixed-value assumptions by 11 using theoretically-grounded, gradient-based importance estimator that efficiently quantifies samples marginal contribution to policy improvement. This innovation integrates data selection as dynamic, self-organized component of the RFT process, forming model-driven curriculum. Furthermore, our constrained optimization procedure for adaptive batch reweighting maximizes the collective contribution of selected samples while ensuring stable policy updates. Extensive experiments demonstrate both the superior performance and high efficiency of our method.
